....?

You seem to not realize that there are components in place to prevent a device from drawing too much power that make that happen. i.e. a PC might only pull 300w and not the entire potential wattage or amperage.

Those systems can be bypassed leading to the device being damaged. Usually by out of specification things. Examples include badly made components/wires, and freak accidents like dropping a hair dryer in water or power surges/brown-outs.

In USB C's case, there are four pins dedicated to power transfer. In an out-of-spec cable, it's entirely possible that power could be transferred on other pins or that the amount is higher than the device expects.

For example, I have my phone. My phone wants 6 watts at 12 volts at 0.5 amps to charge at it's optimal manufacturer specified charge rate.

A badly made cable garbles the sideband info sent from my phone to the device the phone is connected to via USB C. The device thinks I want 60 watts at 12 volts at 5 amps. It gives my phone that. My phone quickly gets hot and either fries and stops receiving power (because the device on the other side thinks it's now disconnected) or it keeps charging until the battery explodes due to heat.

From the Power Delivery specifications:

USB Power Delivery offers the following features:

  • Increased power levels from existing USB standards up to 100W.
  • Power direction is no longer fixed. This enables the product with the power (Host or Peripheral) to provide the power.
  • Optimize power management across multiple peripherals by allowing each device to take only the power it requires, and to get more power when required for a given application.
  • Intelligent and flexible system level management of power via optional hub communication with the PC.
  • Allows low power cases such as headsets to negotiate for only the power they require.

Examples:

  • Enables new higher power use cases such as USB bus powered Hard Disk Drives (HDDs) and printers. This eliminates the need for a separate power brick.
  • A monitor with a supply from the wall can power, or charge, a laptop while still displaying.
  • USB power bricks or chargers are able to supply power through a laptop’s USB ports.
  • Laptops and USB power bricks can provide higher power to battery powered devices (not currently defined by USB).
  • Battery powered devices can get increased charging current from a hub and then give it back temporarily when the user’s HDD requires to spin up.

The bold bit about headsets is an example. If the negotiation for power fails, the device can possibly be fried.

You might say, "Well, TVs and displays aren't low power devices." Yes. But TVs and displays in general don't need 100w. They're fairly power efficient for what they are. See here. Power usage ranges from 20-80w for many computer monitors. Getting more than that could damage the monitor.

Then you have to consider "what if the power regulation in the USB C cable fails?" Meaning, what if, due to a bad USB C cable, more than 100w is supplied (this is the definition of "out of specification"). You're device will be thoroughly screwed and your cable may even get hot and melt (I've had this happen with power cables during power surges).

You seem to not realize basic principals of electricity in addition to how power is delivered and consumed by USB devices. I could build a 1000W 5V micro-usb power adapter and plug it into my phone and the battery would charge just like normal. Just because 1000W is available doesn't mean the phone is going to use it. It's up to the charging circuit in my phone to determine how much power it will draw to safely charge the battery.

Negotiating higher charging rates over USB is just the phone and power supply (PC, laptop, smart adapter, etc) asking each other "are you USB3 (or whatever version) complaint? If so, I'm gonna go ahead and engage my high-rate charging circuit instead of this low-rate default circuit. Yes. OK cool, thanks."
